newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Gazprom bond plans overshadowed by poor shares.
newsitem.headline: Gazprom bond plans overshadowed by poor shares.

text.p: Bold plans by Russian gas group Gazprom to begin a $3 billion capital market borrowing next month are overshadowed by the money-losing performance of its foreign-trading shares, analysts said on Tuesday.

Gazprom plans to eventually issue $2 billion in Eurobonds, one secured by exports, which are likely to be popular and likely to paid off, since Gazprom has a third of the world's gas reserves and accounts for 60 percent of Europe's gas imports.
But RAO Gazprom's slated September issue of a $1 billion bond, likely to convert into American Depositary Shares (ADSs or ADRs), is more complicated.
"It is a question of structure," said Merrill Lynch emerging markets, Europe, Managing Director Dan Lubash.

"Fundamentally, the issue is that now Gazprom is cheap as an asset play, for the ADR or the local share. The problem is psychological because foreigners do not like it that one tranche (of the shares) is pricier than the other."
MC Securities gas analyst Stephen O'Sullivan said investors with long horizons might buy the convertible bond to guarantee short-term performance, betting on conversion at a good price.
But another Western Gazprom analyst dismissed the bond: "Convertible into what -- ADRs? Who wants ADRs -- nobody."
Gazprom is a unique company and has tried to impose its will on equities markets in a way investors have not appreciated.
Foreign investors can legally buy Gazprom only through ADRs which trade at a 100 percent premium to domestic shares, a system the company and government have promised to maintain.
Buying the shares domestically -- something foreigners are not allowed to do -- is also hedged about by restrictions.

About one percent of Gazprom is represented by ADRs, but another 3-7 percent, depending on estimates, is in unapproved grey schemes run by banks for foreign investors. They are not easily accessible but at the least annoying for ADR investors.
Gazprom ADRs have lost money since they were launched 10 months ago in the company's only public funding to date, while the Russian market has tripled in value.
Gazprom ADRs are trading at about $17.30 against $18.50 on October 22. The Russian Trading System index of leading shares rose to 554.20 from 183.72 over the same period.
Gazprom has criticised the organisation of the main domestic equity market, the Russian Trading System, and a presidential decree has stopped its shares trading there.
But chief executive Rem Vyakhirev revealed concern about the impact of this policy, when he complained last week that the price and trading volume of the domestically traded shares were too low.
Foreigners no longer consider the battered shares a proxy for Russia. At best Gazprom equity is now seen as either the only Russia gas sector play or an asset play.
New international standard accounts released in July cleared up the company's financial position but analysts draw sharply different conclusions from the numbers.
The Russian government, scraping for revenues, forced Gazprom to pay 16.5 trillion roubles ($2.8 billion) tax interest and penalties, near double its nine trillion rouble net profit.
Debt ratios are low, with gearing three percent compared to 13-45 percent at major Western energy firms, MC Securities said.
But cash assets are also low, with 57 percent of receivables paid by barter, and low debt ratios may simply reflect generous assumptions on the value of non-cash assets.

"Low net earnings are not reflective of Gazprom as an operating business so much as of an unusual regulatory environment," said a senior Western analyst bullish on Gazprom. "Cash flow will skyrocket as collections improve."

"If you add tax penalties back into net earnings, you have net earnings of well over 20 trillion roubles, which is a really high profit for a company with a market cap of $15 billion (based on local shares) or even $40 billion (based on the ADS)."
MC Securities' O'Sullivan said: "Very long term, this company is very cheap in comparison with other energy companies, but it probably will be next year, too."

Gazprom long-term borrowing has increased substantially this year. It has raised at least $4 billion in syndicated loans and is planning the $3 billion in bonds on top of $2.7 billion in long-term liabilities in the 1996 report.
"One questions investors have to ask is how much more debt can Gazprom raise?" O'Sullivan added. ($ = 5,800 roubles)
